interactions.summary: A student rejects Jiang's strict punishment-versus-allowance frame and asks why therapy or education cannot function as a middle path.
Jiang accepts the therapy premise for the sake of the thought experiment and presses the class to say what bringing in a therapist or police would actually communicate to Eve.
The therapy-defending student answers that therapy has a proven record for severe behavioral conditions, including sociopathy.
Students speculate that a therapist would either side with Eve or interrogate her, and Jiang rejects the first guess while keeping the focus on how therapy would feel to the child.
Jiang concludes that therapy would itself operate as punishment and would teach Eve that her parents prefer handing her off to an outsider rather than bearing the wound themselves.

speaker_notes.note: These two brief answers are clearly student turns, but the diarization does not give enough identity stability to treat them as the same speaker.

claims.claim: A student argues that Jiang's metaphor is too absolute because responsible parenting could include education or therapy rather than only punishment or permissiveness.
The therapy-defending student appeals to modern clinical effectiveness, saying therapy is proven to work across serious conditions including sociopathy.

Jiang refuses to let the discussion become a generic defense of therapy and instead asks what outsourcing the response to a therapist or police would mean inside the emotional logic of the thought experiment.
Students infer that therapeutic intervention would be uncomfortable for Eve, whether because the therapist sides against the parent or because the session becomes an invasive interrogation.

Jiang argues that therapy would function as punishment because pills or outside discipline would tell Eve that her parents prefer delegating the problem to a stranger instead of personally proving love.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang keeps the atonement metaphor alive by converting a modern therapy objection into a question about what outsourced care actually says to the guilty child.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I'm going to call the therapist. The therapist will come and solve this problem with me.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet's turn from doctrinal argument into a fight over whether delegated expertise can carry the same redemptive meaning as parental sacrifice.

signature_moments.moment: Therapy gets reframed as a sign that the parents have chosen an outsider over the child.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Her parents love the therapist. They probably don't love her.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's sharpest compression of why delegation breaks the sacrificial logic he wants the class to see.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang uses the phrase to argue that outside treatment would still register to Eve as punitive delegation rather than loving reconciliation.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet marks the pivot from Jiang's dog-sacrifice explanation of atonement to a class dispute over whether modern therapeutic delegation can replace sacrificial parental response.

uncertainty_notes.note: The class answers Jiang's prompt in short fragments, so the exact reasoning behind each student's therapy scenario is only partially developed.
